title: Air Plan Approval; Michigan; Infrastructure SIP Requirements for the 2015 Ozone NAAQS; Michigan State Board Requirements
summary:
Big picture: the government just announced new Postal Service prices and a couple of clean air decisions affecting Michigan and Rhode Island.

On shipping, the Postal Service will raise many package rates. Flat Rate envelopes and boxes are going up, Ground Advantage will be higher overall, and commercial shippers will see larger increases than retail customers. Some extras stay the same, like Pickup on Demand and Tracking Plus, but others will cost more. Adult Signature fees jump notably, and penalties for oversized or poorly measured packages will rise, including the dimension fee doubling to three dollars. The Postal Service is also adding a Delivered Duty Paid option for items sent from certain U.S. territories to the mainland, letting senders prepay duties and taxes so recipients aren’t surprised later. That service won’t be available everywhere at first.

Who benefits here? The Postal Service gets more revenue to support operations, and shippers sending from U.S. territories may appreciate smoother delivery with prepaid duties. Who may feel the pinch? Small businesses, online sellers, and frequent shippers will face higher costs, especially for larger or nonstandard packages. Individual customers mailing holiday gifts will also see higher totals at the counter.

On air quality, the Environmental Protection Agency approved a narrow piece of Michigan’s clean air plan related to how the state handles conflicts of interest for officials who make air decisions. Michigan dissolved certain environmental boards, and the state already has rules to disclose conflicts, so the agency signed off on that part of the plan. This mainly provides regulatory certainty; it doesn’t add new requirements for residents or businesses. Some may welcome the clarity, while others may prefer additional layers of independent oversight.

In Rhode Island, the agency approved the phaseout of older vapor recovery equipment at gas pumps, along with small updates to the rules for storage tanks. Because modern vehicles capture fuel vapors on their own, these systems at the pump are no longer considered necessary in most places. Gas station owners could save on maintenance and upgrade costs, and drivers may not notice any change. Some people may worry about emissions from older vehicles or poorly maintained equipment, but the state and federal rules continue to cover basic pollution controls at stations.

In short, expect higher shipping costs and a new prepaid option for certain territory-to-mainland packages, plus two targeted air policy moves: a Michigan paperwork update and a Rhode Island shift away from outdated gas pump hardware.
